place.zh: 沂中医 · 解剖实验室 · 古籍部
place.en: Yizhong · the anatomy lab · the rare-books room

setup.zh: 默写十二正经交了白卷，当着半个球馆背不出第二条；解剖台上看见了膈肌；图书馆负一层，一个记错朝代的老太太说：先吐。秋分试跑岔了气。
setup.en: A blank sheet for the twelve channels, and he can't recite the second one in front of half the gym; the diaphragm on the dissecting table; in the library basement an old woman who gets her dynasties wrong says: out first. A stitch on the equinox trial run.

recap.zh: 白卷，举着胳膊走三圈背下来了；解剖台上的膈肌；阿禾的挤公交；葛奶奶的《养性延命录》和门边那一函手札：喘不上来，先吐。
recap.en: A blank sheet, then the twelve channels learned with arms raised, three laps; the diaphragm on the table; Ahe's crowded bus; Granny Ge's old book and the boxed notes by the door: when you can't get breath, breathe out first.

zh: 白卷上只剩两个字：沈芒。
膈肌，像一张绷紧的鼓皮。
en: Only two characters left on the blank sheet: his name.
The diaphragm, like a drumskin pulled tight.

story.zh:
开课头一天，一食堂二楼，马小宝的餐盘「咣」地落在他对面：两份红烧肉、一只鸡腿、四个鸡蛋。他一口吃掉一个鸡蛋：「你吃土豆丝？土豆丝长不出肉。」吃完把盘子一推，摸了摸肚子，「还饿。」起身的时候裤兜里滚出一只小白瓶，满瓶身的洋文，他弯腰捡起来，拧开，倒两粒在手心，干咽了：「鱼油，深海鱼的，我妈非让我吃。」又拿筷子敲了敲沈芒的盘沿：「你来球队图什么，我看出来了，她没看出来——她看什么都是数。十月十七试训，你要是过不了，」他笑得很和气，「我替你跟她说。说得好听点，就说有个人，为了她，一千米跑吐了。放心，我嘴严。」

沈芒对着那盘土豆丝坐了很久。这话里没有一个字是吓人的，可他浑身的汗，比早上跑完二十分钟还多。

下午解剖课绪论，老师在黑板上画了一个人，从外往里一层一层地标：皮肤，浅筋膜，深筋膜，肌肉，血管神经，骨头。沈芒举起手：「老师，那经络在第几层？」后排有人「噗」地笑出了声。那位说话很轻的女老师没有笑，想了想：「解剖学到今天，没有找到经络这样一种单独的结构。」她把手里的骨盆模型放下，又道：「两千多年前没有解剖刀，古人只有手。按这儿，酸麻往那儿走；扎这儿，那儿的疼轻了；摸脉，一跳一跳，连着。一处一处记下来，连成线——长沙马王堆出土的帛书上，还只有十一条，后来才凑成十二条，配一年十二个月。」她顿了顿，「这几十年，有人顺着线切开看，有人往穴位里打同位素，有人说找着了一种细管子，别人照着再做，做不出来。切开了，是血管、神经、筋膜，各走各的。」她拿粉笔在黑板上画了一个省的轮廓：「经络像地图上这条省界。地上挖不出这条线，可你过了界，口音就变了。」

沈芒坐下了，脑子里嗡嗡的。周四要默的那十二样东西，原来是十二样谁也没见过的东西。

此后三夜，六一七熄灯以后，下铺一直在念经。念到第五条，前四条就开始往外漏，像一只底下有洞的口袋。眼镜递过来一张学长传下的口诀：「肺大胃脾心小肠，膀肾包焦胆肝续。」沈芒念了十遍，口诀记住了，一到默的时候脑子里只剩四个字：包子焦了。老蔡在上铺听不下去了：「你这么背不行。十二正经就是十二条河，奇经八脉是水库。河里的水满了往水库里流，水库满了，人就飞了。」「又飞了。」「不飞你修它干嘛？」

周二晚上他去图书馆找带图的书，开架书库里真有一本《经络腧穴图谱》，一个光头小人身上画满了红线绿线，像一张公交线路图，线路全，哪一路先发哪一路后发，不写。下楼时他走错了楼梯，一直走到负一层。楼道尽头一道灰色的防火门，门上贴着一张纸：「古籍部（善本阅览室）　凭证入内　只许抄阅，不许外借」。门缝底下渗出一股凉气。他从小看的修仙小说里都有一句老话：真功法，都藏在没人翻的古书里。他伸手去推，门禁「嘀」地一声，红灯。那道门，他记住了。

找不着，默写照样要默。礼拜四上午，针灸推拿学导论，[严老师]{注=jin-yan}在黑板上写了一行，粉笔敲得笃笃响：

「[经脉者，所以能决死生，处百病，调虚实，不可不通。]{典=lingshu-jingmai}」

「收书，默写十二正经。」他背着手一排一排地走，「去年有人抄在胳膊上。」

沈芒左胳膊里侧，细笔抄着十二行。他把手揣进桌肚，拿唾沫使劲搓，搓完一看，十二行糊成了一片蓝。他拿起笔，写下「手太阴肺经」，然后发现，他只记得这一条。黑板上那一行字的末了四个字正对着他的座位：不可不通。

严老师翻到一张，停住，举起来：「沈芒。白卷。」后排有人笑。「十二条都背不下来的，可以早点想想，是不是走错了门。」

卷子发回来，只剩右上角两个字：沈芒。他叠了两叠，塞进兜里最深处，像是怕谁看见。心里有个声音在说：沈芒啊沈芒，一个找不着的东西，你也记不住。

下午五点，球馆。训练刚散，马小宝摇着大摇杯晃过来，冲场边嚷了一嗓子：「领队，听说咱们新人今天交了白卷？」阿禾正低着头写字，没抬头。马小宝拍拍沈芒的肩：「来，背一个给领队听听。就背第二条。」

半个球馆的人都停了手。沈芒张开嘴：「手太阴肺经……手……」后头没有了。那一溜蓝字糊在他袖子里，口诀在他脑子里，「肺大」后头该接哪一条，怎么也接不上。他站在那里，嘴张着，像礼拜一坐进红圈的那一下，又坐了一回。脸从耳根烧到脖子，他能听见自己的心跳，一下一下撞着嗓子眼。马小宝也不笑，弯下腰凑到他耳朵边，声音压得很低：「十二条都背不下来，十月十七，还过得去？我那句话，可还算数。」说罢直起身，晃着摇杯走了。

阿禾这才抬起头，看了他一眼，在本子上写了一笔。写的什么，他不敢看。

那夜他没背书。他把书摊在桌上，翻到那张小人图，站到宿舍正中，两只胳膊举过头顶——图上那个小人，就是这么举着的。

他从胸口找起：锁骨底下一寸，手太阴肺经从这儿出来，顺着胳膊里侧往上走，走到大拇指尖。大拇指挨着食指，手阳明大肠经接住了，顺着胳膊外侧往下，翻过肩膀，落到鼻子旁边。鼻子旁边，足阳明胃经接过去，从脸上往下，过胸，过肚子，过膝盖前头，落到第二个脚趾。第二个脚趾挨着大脚趾，足太阴脾经接住，又顺着腿里侧往上，回到了胸口。

他的手停在胸口，愣住了。回来了。

他接着比第二圈：胸口出来，到小指；小指翻到手背，下来到耳朵前头；眼角里头起，翻过头顶，顺着后背一路往下，到小脚趾；脚底板再往上，又回到胸口——这一圈，全走在背后。第三圈：胸口到中指；无名指下来，到眉梢；眼角外头起，顺着身子两侧往下，到第四个脚趾；大脚趾再往上，回到胸口，又接上了肺经。

他站在那儿，两只胳膊还举着，忽然全明白了。举着手，阴经全往上走，阳经全往下走；手指尖上、脚趾尖上，阴阳换手；脸上，阳经跟阳经换手；胸口里，阴经跟阴经换手。哪里是十二条各管各的线——是一条，绕着人跑三圈：头一圈走前面，第二圈走后面，第三圈走两边。像一班接力的人，跑一圈又回来，把棒子交到下一个人手里。

眼镜在对面床上，把眼镜往上一推：「……你再比一遍，我录下来。」老蔡也跟着举起胳膊，在上铺比划到第四条，胳膊撞上了天花板，「哎哟」一声：「我这个上铺，阳经走不下去。」

他闭上眼睛，又比了一遍，一条没错。第二天上午重默，过了。严老师在那张纸上批了个「过」，看了他一眼，没说别的。他把九月十七那张白卷从兜里掏出来，展平了，白的一面朝外，贴在节气挂图旁边。眼镜道：「贴反了。」沈芒道：「没反。白的这一面，是给我自己看的。」

九月二十一日，星期一，下午两点，实验楼五楼。沈芒头一回进解剖实验室。

门一推开，先出来的是一股福尔马林的味儿，冲得人还没进门，眼泪先下来了。四十个穿白大褂的大一新生挤在门口，谁也不肯头一个进去。屋里六张台子，每张台子上盖着一块白布，白布底下，是一个人的形状。他站在最后一排，两只手在白大褂兜里攥成了拳头。离补测还有三天；离他头一回看见一个死了的人，还有十步。

台脚边一张塑封卡片，那位说话很轻的女老师弯下腰念：「刘桂芝，女，七十九岁。生前是小学老师。她留了一句话：让孩子们别怕，好好学。」四十个人弯下腰去，沈芒弯得最深，深到看见了自己的鞋尖。他心里乱糟糟的，最后只想了一句：刘老师，我胆子小，您多担待。

老师管她叫「大体老师」：「这是你们头一位老师，一句话不说，教你们一学期。」规矩也是她当场讲的：不许拍照，不许说笑；白布只揭开今天要看的那一块，别处盖好；切下来的，哪怕指甲盖大一小片，也要放回原处——学期末，大体老师要囫囵个儿地送去火化，每年清明，学校还给她们开追思会。两层口罩也挡不住那股味儿；第一节课下来，好几个人一个礼拜没吃肉。

这一节看胸腔。白布掀开一角，胸口是预先打开的，两叶肺拨到两边，塌着，颜色比他想的深。沈芒原以为自己要吐——他连塑料袋都揣好了，跟上回阿禾塞给他的那只一模一样，特意去超市买的——可他没吐。他只是看着，看着看着，就忘了怕。

老师拿镊子指着肺底下横着的一大片肉，薄薄的，往上拱，像一顶倒扣的帐篷：「膈肌。胸和肚子之间的这一张，就是它。你吸一口气，主要是它在干活：它一收，这顶帐篷往下压平，胸腔底下空出地方，肺就被拽着鼓起来；它往下一压，肚子里的东西没处去，肚子就往外鼓。它一松，弹回去，气就出来了。你们这会儿每喘一口，都是它在动。一天，两万来下。」

她叫人上前，戴着手套，拿指头轻轻按一按。轮到沈芒，他的手抖了一下，按下去——不像肉，像一张绷紧了的鼓皮，又薄又韧。他缩回手，低头看了看自己的肚子，想起那一千米：肩膀一耸一耸，脖子上的筋鼓着，胸口起得又快又浅——可他的肚子，从头到尾，一动都没动过。

「老师，」他举手，「要是一个人喘气，光动胸口，肚子不动呢？」

老师看了他一眼，认出来了，是上礼拜问经络在第几层的那个。「那就是这块大肌肉在偷懒，」她道，「让脖子和肩膀上那几块小肌肉替它干。小肌肉干不了大活，一口气吸不深。」

下课铃响了。沈芒最后一个出实验室，在门口回头，又朝那张台子鞠了一躬。

傍晚他一个人去体育场，要拿肚子喘。头一圈他使劲想着那顶帐篷：吸，往下压；吐，弹回来。想着想着，脚步乱了，左脚右脚商量不好谁先走；再想着想着，他发现自己连喘气都不会了——喘了十八年从来没想过它，一想，倒忘了怎么喘。阿禾从跑道边上过，站住了：「你干嘛呢？」

「练膈肌。」

「反了。你一吸，肚子往里收。」他低头一看，可不是，胸口一挺，像一只受了惊的鸽子。

「人一慌，就这么喘，又浅又快。」阿禾道，「每口气总有一截堵在喉咙、气管里，到不了肺，下一口又原样吐出来——跟挤公交一样，门口那一截人永远进不了车厢。喘得越浅越快，白喘得越多。你那天第四百米，一半是白喘。」

「那怎么办？」

「门口那截人，先下车。」她合上本子走了，走出几步又回头，「礼拜四下午四点。三天改不好喘气，别硬改，还不如不改。」

沈芒站在跑道上，两手叉着腰。不改，就是九月十一号那个样子；改，三天改不好。知道了是膈肌偷懒，可怎么叫它不偷懒，没人教。门口那截人怎么下车，她也没说。

九月二十二日下午，他在图书馆负一层那道灰色防火门前站了二十分钟。门禁是红灯。他正要走，门从里头开了，出来一个[老太太]{注=jin-ge}，七十来岁，蓝布套袖，老花镜挂在链子上，手里捏着一支铅笔：「在门口晃了二十分钟。我从监控里看着呢，还以为是偷书的。偷书的没你这么老实。」

「奶奶，有没有那种……一般人看不懂、看懂了就特别厉害的书？」

「有。」老太太道，「字典。」

沈芒脸一红，老老实实道：「……讲喘气的。」

她眯起眼睛看了他一会儿，转身往里走：「进来。包存外头柜子里。笔，只许用铅笔。书，只许抄，不许借。说话小点声，书怕吵。」古籍部恒温恒湿，常年二十来度，从九月的大太阳底下一脚踏进来，胳膊上的汗毛都站了起来。她姓葛，说葛洪是她们老葛家的，五百年前是一家。她先叫他去水池边洗两遍手——「手上有油，纸记仇，三十年后还看得出你的指头印」——一面找书一面说话，说这屋子的空调比他岁数还大，说她那只猫叫「善本」，因为也只许看不许抱，说她年轻时在修复室裱书，一张宋版的纸补了三个月……沈芒听着，觉得她一句也没说到喘气上。

她捧出一函线装书：「陶弘景，《养性延命录》。唐朝的，山中宰相——皇帝有事，跑到山里去问他。」竖排繁体，一页全讲怎么往外出气：吹、呼、唏、呵、嘘、呬，六个字个个认得，连在一块儿一句不懂。他认到一句，停住了：

「[凡人极者，则多嘘呬。]{典=yangxing-liuzi}」

人累到了头，就多嘘、多呬。他蹲在跑道边上一口一口往外吐的，可不就是这个。原来一千五百年前，就有人看见过他。

函套里夹着一张发黄的借阅卡。一九七几年几格钢笔字；一九八几年，一个名字连着登了十几格，字写得很小，很急，后来洇了水，认不出了；再往下，一格也没有。「三十多年没人翻过它，」葛奶奶在他身后道，「你是头一个。登上。」他在头一个空格里写下「沈芒，2026.9.22」，看着上头那个名字，心里动了一下。

葛奶奶把函套合上，像是顺嘴：「这一函讲的，就是先吐。吐干净了，它自己就进来了。」

门口那截人，先下车。他站在那儿，半天没动。

取包的时候，他蹲到门边那架矮书架前头。最底层横着一函旧书，函套磨得发白，签条掉了；解开，里头八册，每册都有两指厚，书脊上只有墨笔写的「一」到「八」。他抽出头一册，扉页上六个毛笔字：《九鼎真人手札》。翻开，头一行：

「余少时，人呼为漏勺。」

沈芒「噗」地笑出了声。一个真人，开口先管自己叫漏勺——这老头有意思。往下翻，不是功法，是日记，一条一条，短得像记账。翻到一条：「是冬，学吐纳。鹅毛日日飞。」他的心跳快了一下——鹅毛，他认得这个，眼镜那本《抱朴子》里有一根。隔了几页，单单一行：「修仙先修心。」

他把这一行看了三遍。他从小看的小说里，真功法的头一页都是这么写的。这老头是真的。他把头一册塞回函里，塞得跟原先一样，心里却记下了：还要来。

回宿舍的路上，他攥着抄了字的纸，到了三号楼底下，抬头看了看六楼。报到那天他在三栋楼里爬了十八层，爬一层，喘一层。他开始往上爬，一边爬，一边不出声地往外吐：两级台阶吐，两级台阶吸，吐要吐干净。到六楼，他站在六一七门口扶着门框——不是喘得要扶，是不敢信。喘是喘的，可那口气是深的，一口顶一口，不往嗓子眼里挤。

他推门进去：「我刚才爬六楼，没喘。」老蔡头也不抬：「你爬六楼，什么时候喘过？」「……报到那天。」「那是十八楼。」

那夜熄了灯，他仰面躺着，肚皮上压一本一千多页的《正常人体解剖学》。「呵——」长长吐干净，书往下沉；鼻子吸，书慢慢升上去。吐到第七口，肚子往下一瘪，底下跟着「噗——」一声，声音很小。沈芒心想：应该没人注意。老蔡在上铺躺不住了，「噌」地探下半个身子，捏着鼻子：「沈忙，你漏气了？」对床的眼镜「哈哈哈哈」笑得直拍床板，笑够了，才道：「我查了。陶弘景是南朝梁的，不是唐朝。葛洪也不是五百年前，是一千七百来年。」沈芒道：「朝代记错了。那一句，没错。」

老蔡忽然从上铺翻了下来，光着脚站在地上，两眼放光：「你这是吐纳！教我！」沈芒道：「这个吹不秃山头。后天，能叫我跑完一千米，不吐。」老蔡想了想，觉得这也是一种神通，回铺上找出一本最厚的书压在自己肚皮上。于是那一夜，六一七黑地里此起彼伏：「呵——」「嘘——」。隔壁六一八敲了三回墙，第三回那边喊过来：「你们宿舍谁在吹气球？」

九月二十三日，秋分。下午他去体育场试跑六百，照明天的速度。头两百米好好的，肚子鼓起来、瘪下去，那本解剖书压出来的路子，竟真的走上了腿。他心里一喜，喜得忘了数步子，一口气吸得太猛，吸到了底——三百米上，右边肋骨底下「嘎嘣」一下，像有人从里头拿针扎了他一下。

岔气了。他捂着肋下，弯着腰一步一步挪到草坪边上坐下，疼得不敢喘，越不敢喘，越疼。

马小宝正在跑道上练折返冲刺，一趟一趟跑得像一辆小卡车。他冲到这头，看见草坪上缩成一团的沈芒，慢下来，蹲下：「岔气了？明天补测七个人。我赌你第七——倒数第一。赌一箱蛋白粉：你不是第七，箱子归你。」他拍拍沈芒的脸，「是第七，十月十七你也别来了，省得我当着她的面，替你说那句话。」说罢一转身，又冲回跑道上去了。

沈芒坐在草坪上，心里冷冰冰地往下沉。六百米都跑不下来，明天是一千米；看台上有人举手机，跑道边上有阿禾的本子，终点上有雷老师的秒表。沈芒啊沈芒，人家古人教你喘气，你喘出个岔气来。

他想起葛奶奶那一句。他不吸了，张开嘴往外吐——不使劲，就那么慢慢地、长长地吐，「嘘——」，吐到吐不动，停一停，让那口气自己进来；再吐。一口，两口，三口。按着肋下的那只手底下，那根针，一点一点地退了出去。

疼是退了。可他坐在那儿，一直坐到天黑，也没敢再站起来跑一步。那一夜他躺在下铺，手心一阵一阵地出汗：明天要是又吐了，年级群里的视频就有下集了。
story.en:
First day of classes, second floor of Canteen One: Ma Xiaobao's tray came down opposite his with a bang — two portions of braised pork, a chicken leg, four eggs. He ate an egg in one bite: "You're eating shredded potato? Potato won't grow muscle." He pushed the emptied tray away and rubbed his belly, "Still hungry." As he got up a little white bottle rolled out of his pocket, covered in foreign writing; he bent, picked it up, unscrewed it, tipped two into his palm and swallowed them dry: "Fish oil, from deep-sea fish. My mum makes me take it." Then he tapped Shen Mang's tray with his chopsticks: "What you're in the team for, I've worked out, and she hasn't — she sees everything as numbers. Trials, October seventeenth; if you don't pass," he smiled very pleasantly, "I'll tell her for you. I'll put it nicely: there's a guy who threw up over a thousand metres for you. Don't worry, I can keep a secret."

Shen Mang sat over his shredded potato for a long time. Not one word of it was frightening, and he sweated more than after the morning's twenty minutes.

In the afternoon, the anatomy introduction. The lecturer drew a person on the board and labelled it layer by layer from the outside in: skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia, muscle, vessels and nerves, bone. Shen Mang raised his hand: "Then which layer are the channels in?" Somebody at the back snorted. The soft-spoken woman didn't laugh; she thought: "To this day anatomy has not found any separate structure that is a channel." She set down the pelvis model. "Two thousand years ago there was no scalpel; the ancients had hands. Press here, and the aching travels there; needle here, and the pain there eases; take the pulse, beat by beat, connected. They noted it place by place and joined it into lines — the silk texts dug up at Mawangdui in Changsha still have only eleven; twelve came later, to match the twelve months." She paused. "Over the last few decades people have cut along the lines, injected isotopes into points, claimed to find a kind of fine tube that nobody else could reproduce. Cut open, it's vessels, nerves, fascia, each going its own way." She chalked the outline of a province on the board: "A channel is like this provincial border on a map. You can't dig the line out of the ground; but cross it, and the accent changes."

Shen Mang sat down with his head buzzing. The twelve things he had to write out on Thursday were twelve things nobody had ever seen.

For three nights after lights-out the bottom bunk recited. By the fifth channel the first four were leaking out, like a bag with a hole in the bottom. Glasses passed him a mnemonic handed down from seniors: "Lung, Large, Stomach, Spleen, Heart, Small Intestine; Bladder, Kidney, Pericardium, Sanjiao, Gall, Liver." Shen Mang said it ten times, remembered the rhyme, and the moment he tried to write, all his head held was: the buns are burnt. Old Cai couldn't stand it any longer from above: "That's no way to learn. The twelve channels are twelve rivers; the eight extraordinary vessels are reservoirs. When the rivers are full they run into the reservoirs, and when the reservoirs are full, you fly." "Flying again." "What are you cultivating them for if not to fly?"

On Tuesday night he went to the library for a book with pictures; the open stacks really had an Atlas of Channels and Points, a bald little man covered in red and green lines like a bus map — every route there, and not a word about which bus leaves first. Coming down he took the wrong staircase and ended up on floor minus one. At the end of the corridor was a grey fire door with a sign: "Rare Books (Special Collections Reading Room) · Card holders only · Copying permitted, no borrowing". A chill seeped from under the door. Every cultivation novel he'd read as a boy had the same old line: the real techniques are in the old books nobody opens. He pushed; the lock beeped, red. He remembered that door.

Found or not, the dictation still had to be written. Thursday morning, Introduction to Acupuncture and Tuina: Teacher Yan wrote a line on the board, the chalk rapping:

"The channels are what decide life and death, treat all diseases, and regulate deficiency and excess; they must not fail to be open."

"Books away. Write out the twelve regular channels." He walked the rows with his hands behind his back. "Last year someone copied them onto his arm."

On the inside of Shen Mang's left forearm, in fine pen, were twelve lines. He pushed the hand into the desk and scrubbed hard with spit; when he looked, the twelve lines had smeared into a single blue patch. He picked up his pen and wrote "Lung channel of hand-Taiyin", and then discovered that was the only one he remembered. The last four characters of the line on the board faced his seat: must not fail to be open.

Teacher Yan turned to one sheet, stopped, held it up: "Shen Mang. Blank." Someone at the back laughed. "Anyone who can't memorise twelve might think early about whether he's walked through the wrong door."

The sheet came back with only two characters in the corner: Shen Mang. He folded it twice and pushed it deep into his pocket, as if afraid someone would see. A voice inside said: Shen Mang, oh Shen Mang — a thing nobody can find, and you can't even remember it.

Five p.m., the gym. Practice had just broken up when Ma Xiaobao sauntered over shaking his big bottle and called to the sideline: "Captain-manager, I hear our new recruit handed in a blank sheet today?" Ahe was writing with her head down and didn't look up. Ma Xiaobao patted Shen Mang's shoulder: "Come on, recite one for the manager. Just the second one."

Half the gym stopped. Shen Mang opened his mouth: "Lung channel of hand-Taiyin... hand..." Nothing followed. The blue smear was in his sleeve, the rhyme was in his head, and what came after "Lung, Large" would not connect. He stood there with his mouth open, like Monday's fall into the red circle all over again. The heat ran from his ears to his neck, and he could hear his heart knocking at his throat. Ma Xiaobao didn't laugh; he bent to his ear, voice low: "Can't memorise twelve — are you going to get through October seventeenth? My offer stands." He straightened and ambled off with his bottle.

Only then did Ahe look up, give him one glance, and write a line in her notebook. What it said, he didn't dare look.

That night he didn't study. He spread the book on the desk, open at the diagram of the little man, stood in the middle of the room and raised both arms over his head — the little man in the picture held his arms just so.

He started from the chest: an inch below the collarbone, the Lung channel of hand-Taiyin comes out here and runs up the inside of the arm to the tip of the thumb. The thumb touches the index finger, and the Large Intestine channel of hand-Yangming takes over, down the outside of the arm, over the shoulder, to beside the nose. Beside the nose the Stomach channel of foot-Yangming takes it, down the face, over the chest, over the belly, past the front of the knee, to the second toe. The second toe touches the big toe, and the Spleen channel of foot-Taiyin takes over, up the inside of the leg, back to the chest.

His hand stopped at his chest, and he froze. It came back.

He went on with the second circuit: out of the chest to the little finger; from the little finger over to the back of the hand and down to the front of the ear; from the inner corner of the eye up over the crown of the head, all the way down the back to the little toe; from the sole back up to the chest — this circuit all ran behind. The third: chest to the middle finger; from the ring finger down to the end of the eyebrow; from the outer corner of the eye down the sides of the body to the fourth toe; from the big toe back up to the chest, joining the Lung channel again.

He stood there with both arms still raised and suddenly understood all of it. Arms up, the yin channels all run upward and the yang channels all downward; at the fingertips and toes, yin hands over to yang; on the face, yang hands over to yang; in the chest, yin hands over to yin. These weren't twelve lines each minding its own business — it was one line, running three laps round a person: the first lap down the front, the second down the back, the third down the sides. Like a relay team, running a lap and coming back to pass the baton to the next runner.

From the bed opposite, Glasses pushed his spectacles up: "...Do that once more. I'm recording it." Old Cai raised his arms too and got as far as the fourth channel on the top bunk before his arm hit the ceiling: "Ow. On a top bunk the yang channels can't go down."

He shut his eyes and traced them all again, not one wrong. The next morning he redid the dictation, and passed. Teacher Yan wrote "pass" on the sheet, gave him a look, and said nothing else. He took the blank sheet from September 17th out of his pocket, smoothed it flat, and pinned it blank side out beside the solar-terms chart. Glasses said: "You've pinned it backwards." Shen Mang said: "No. The blank side is for me to look at."

September 21st, Monday, two in the afternoon, fifth floor of the laboratory building. Shen Mang's first time in the anatomy lab.

The door opened and formalin came out first, so sharp that the tears came before anyone was through it. Forty first-years in white coats bunched in the doorway and nobody would go in first. Inside were six tables, each under a white sheet, and under each sheet the shape of a person. He stood in the last row with both hands clenched into fists in his coat pockets. Three days to the retest; ten steps to the first time he would see a dead person.

A laminated card stood at the foot of the table, and the soft-spoken woman bent and read it: "Liu Guizhi, female, seventy-nine. A primary-school teacher in life. She left one sentence: tell the children not to be afraid, and to study well." Forty people bowed; Shen Mang bowed deepest, deep enough to see his own shoe tips. His mind was a jumble; in the end he thought one thing: Teacher Liu, I'm a coward, please bear with me.

The lecturer called her a "silent teacher" — the body donor: "This is your first teacher. She says nothing, and teaches you for a whole term." She laid down the rules there and then: no photos, no joking; lift the sheet only from the part being studied today and keep the rest covered; anything cut away, even a piece the size of a fingernail, goes back where it belongs — at the end of term the silent teachers go whole to cremation, and every Qingming the university holds a memorial for them. Two masks couldn't keep the smell out; after the first class several people went a week without eating meat.

This session was the chest. A corner of the sheet lifted: the chest had been opened in advance, the two lungs drawn to either side, collapsed, darker than he'd imagined. Shen Mang had been sure he would be sick — he'd brought a plastic bag, the same kind Ahe had pushed into his hand, bought specially at the supermarket — but he wasn't. He only looked, and as he looked he forgot to be afraid.

The lecturer pointed with her forceps at the broad thin sheet of muscle lying beneath the lungs, domed upward like an upturned tent: "The diaphragm. This is the sheet between chest and belly. When you breathe in, this is what does most of the work: it contracts, the tent flattens downward, space opens at the bottom of the chest, and the lungs are pulled open; as it presses down, what's in the belly has nowhere to go, so the belly swells out. It relaxes, springs back, and the air comes out. Every breath you take right now, it's moving. Twenty thousand or so times a day."

She called people up to press it gently, gloved. When it was Shen Mang's turn his hand shook once and then pressed — not like flesh, like a drumskin stretched tight, thin and tough. He drew his hand back and looked down at his own belly, and thought of that thousand metres: shoulders heaving, the cords of his neck standing out, chest rising fast and shallow — and his belly, from first to last, never moving once.

"Miss," he put up his hand, "what if someone breathes with only the chest moving, and the belly not at all?"

She looked at him and recognised him — the one who'd asked which layer the channels were in. "Then this big muscle is slacking," she said, "and the small muscles in the neck and shoulders are doing its job. Small muscles can't do big work; the breath can't go deep."

The bell went. Shen Mang was last out of the lab, and at the door he turned and bowed to that table once more.

That evening he went to the sports field alone, to breathe with his belly. For the first lap he thought hard about the tent: in, press down; out, spring back. Thinking about it, his feet got muddled, left and right unable to agree who went first; thinking harder, he found he no longer knew how to breathe at all — eighteen years of breathing without once thinking about it, and one thought undid it. Ahe came past the track and stopped: "What are you doing?"

"Training my diaphragm."

"Backwards. When you breathe in, your belly goes in." He looked down — so it did, chest thrust out like a startled pigeon.

"When people panic they breathe like that, shallow and fast," Ahe said. "In every breath there's a stretch that's stuck in the throat and windpipe and never reaches the lungs, and goes straight back out with the next breath — like a crowded bus: the people jammed in the doorway never get into the carriage. The shallower and faster you breathe, the more of it is wasted. At four hundred metres that day, half your breathing was waste."

"So what do I do?"

"The people in the doorway get off first." She closed her notebook and walked on, then turned back: "Thursday, four p.m. Three days isn't enough to fix your breathing — don't force it. Better not to change than to change badly."

Shen Mang stood on the track with his hands on his hips. Don't change, and it's September 11th all over again; change, and three days isn't enough. He knew the diaphragm was slacking; how to make it work, nobody had taught him. How the people in the doorway get off, she hadn't said either.

On the afternoon of September 22nd he stood for twenty minutes in front of that grey fire door on floor minus one of the library. The lock showed red. He was about to leave when the door opened from inside and out came an old woman in her seventies, blue cloth oversleeves, reading glasses on a chain, a pencil in her hand: "Twenty minutes hovering out there. I've been watching you on the camera — thought you were a book thief. A book thief wouldn't look so honest."

"Granny, is there a book that... ordinary people can't understand, and if you do understand it you're really something?"

"There is," the old woman said. "The dictionary."

Shen Mang went red and said honestly: "...about breathing."

She narrowed her eyes at him a moment, then turned inside: "Come in. Bag in the lockers outside. Pencils only. Books are copied, not borrowed. Keep your voice down; books don't like noise." The rare-books room was climate-controlled, twenty degrees all year; one step in from the September sun and the hairs on his arms stood up. Her surname was Ge, and she said Ge Hong was one of her Ges — same family five hundred years back. She made him wash his hands twice at the sink first — "oil on your hands and the paper bears a grudge; thirty years on it still shows your fingerprints" — and talked while she looked for the book: the air conditioning here was older than he was; her cat was called Rare Edition, because it too could be looked at but not held; when she was young she'd mounted books in the restoration room and spent three months patching one sheet of Song paper... Shen Mang listened and felt she had not said one word about breathing.

She brought out a boxed thread-bound set: "Tao Hongjing, the Yangxing Yanming Lu. Tang dynasty, the Prime Minister in the Mountains — when the emperor had a problem he went up the mountain to ask him." Vertical columns, traditional characters, a whole page on breathing out: chui, hu, xi, he, xu, xi — six characters he knew one by one and couldn't make a sentence of together. He came to one line and stopped:

"Whenever a man is at the end of his strength, he does much xu and xi."

When a man is at the end of his strength he does much xu and xi — breathes out hard and long. Crouched at the edge of the track breathing it out mouthful by mouthful, that was exactly what he'd done. Fifteen hundred years ago, someone had already seen him.

In the case was a yellowed borrowing card. A few boxes from the nineteen-seventies in fountain pen; then, in the eighties, one name signed a dozen boxes in a row, the writing small and hurried, later blurred by water until it couldn't be read; after that, nothing. "Thirty-odd years and no one's opened it," Granny Ge said behind him. "You're the first. Sign." In the first empty box he wrote "Shen Mang, 2026.9.22", looked at the name above, and something in him stirred.

Granny Ge closed the case, as if in passing: "What this set teaches is: out first. Empty it right out, and the next one comes in by itself."

The people in the doorway get off first. He stood there a long moment without moving.

Collecting his bag, he crouched by the low shelf beside the door. Across the bottom shelf lay a boxed set of old books, the case worn white, its label gone; opened, eight volumes, each two fingers thick, with only "one" to "eight" in ink on the spines. He drew out the first; on the flyleaf, six brushed characters: Notes of the True Man of the Nine Cauldrons. He opened it; the first line:

"When I was young, people called me the Leaky Ladle."

Shen Mang snorted with laughter. A True Man who opened by calling himself a leaky ladle — this old fellow was fun. Further in, not techniques but a diary, entry after entry, short as a ledger. He came to one: "That winter, learned breathing. The goose feather flew every day." His heart gave a quick beat — a goose feather; he knew that one, there was one in Glasses's Baopuzi. A few pages on, one line alone: "To cultivate immortality, first cultivate the heart."

He read that line three times. Every novel he'd read as a boy had put exactly that on the first page of the real technique. This old man was the real thing. He slid the first volume back into the case, exactly as it had been, and noted inside: come back.

On the way back to the dorm, clutching the sheet he'd copied, he reached the foot of Building Three and looked up at the sixth floor. On registration day he had climbed eighteen floors across three buildings, panting on every one. He started up, and as he climbed he breathed out without a sound: two steps out, two steps in, out all the way. At the sixth floor he stood at the door of 617 holding the frame — not because he had to, but because he didn't believe it. He was breathing hard, yes, but the breath was deep, one breath worth one breath, not jammed in his throat.

He pushed the door open: "I just climbed six floors without panting." Old Cai didn't look up: "When did you ever pant climbing six floors?" "...Registration day." "That was eighteen."

That night after lights-out he lay on his back with the thousand-page Normal Human Anatomy on his belly. "Haaa —" a long breath out to empty, and the book sank; in through the nose, and the book slowly rose. On the seventh breath, as his belly went down, a small "pfft" followed from below. Shen Mang thought: nobody will have noticed. Old Cai couldn't stay still above him, swung half his body down, nose pinched: "Shen Busy, are you leaking?" Across the room Glasses laughed "hahaha" and slapped his bed boards, and when he'd finished said: "I looked it up. Tao Hongjing is Southern Liang, not Tang. And Ge Hong isn't five hundred years back, more like seventeen hundred." Shen Mang said: "She got the dynasties wrong. The sentence was right."

Old Cai suddenly tumbled down from the top bunk and stood barefoot on the floor, eyes shining: "That's breath cultivation! Teach me!" Shen Mang said: "This won't blow a mountaintop bald. Day after tomorrow, it'll get me through a thousand metres without throwing up." Old Cai considered that a kind of magic too, climbed back up and found his thickest book to put on his own belly. So that night 617 breathed in the dark, back and forth: "Haaa —" "Shhh —". Room 618 knocked on the wall three times, and on the third shouted through: "Who in your room is blowing up balloons?"

September 23rd, the Autumn Equinox. In the afternoon he went to the field to run six hundred at tomorrow's pace. The first two hundred went fine: belly out, belly in, the path the anatomy book had pressed into him had actually got into his legs. He was so pleased he forgot to count his steps, drew one breath too hard, right to the bottom — and at three hundred metres something went "crack" under his right ribs, like a needle driven in from inside.

A stitch. Clutching his side, bent double, he shuffled to the grass and sat; it hurt too much to breathe, and the less he dared breathe the more it hurt.

Ma Xiaobao was doing shuttle sprints on the track, back and forth like a small truck. He reached this end, saw Shen Mang curled up on the grass, slowed, and squatted: "Stitch? Seven of you in the retest tomorrow. I'm betting you come seventh — last. A case of protein powder: if you're not seventh, it's yours." He patted Shen Mang's cheek. "If you are, don't bother coming on October seventeenth either — save me telling her that in front of her face." He turned and sprinted back onto the track.

Shen Mang sat on the grass with a cold weight sinking in him. He couldn't get through six hundred, and tomorrow was a thousand; phones raised in the stand, Ahe's notebook at the trackside, Mr Lei's stopwatch at the finish. Shen Mang, oh Shen Mang — the ancients teach you to breathe and you breathe yourself a stitch.

He thought of Granny Ge's sentence. He stopped breathing in and opened his mouth to breathe out — no force, just slowly, long, "shhh —", out until he couldn't, pause, let the breath come in on its own; out again. One, two, three. Under the hand pressed to his side, the needle withdrew a little at a time.

The pain went. But he sat there until dark and didn't dare stand and run another step. That night in the bottom bunk his palms sweated in waves: if he threw up again tomorrow, the year-group video would have a sequel.

exits.means: goes to the retest on the twenty-fourth
